presentingComplaint: Brought from home with 1 day of rigors, drowsiness and a rising, foul, turbid output in his long-term urinary catheter bag.
history: Chronic indwelling urethral catheter for 14 months following management of neurogenic bladder and prior acute urinary retention; catheter last changed 6 weeks ago and never flushed since. Over the preceding 18 hours he developed shaking chills, reduced urine output, and progressive confusion noted by his daughter. No cough, no abdominal pain, no diarrhoea. Type 2 diabetes and hypertension. No known drug allergy. No antibiotics or hospital admission in the last 90 days and no prior resistant-organism isolates. On admission he was hypotensive and lactate-elevated; despite a 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus his mean arterial pressure remained below 65 mmHg, so a noradrenaline infusion was commenced. Blood and catheter-specimen cultures were drawn and the chronic catheter was removed and replaced with a fresh catheter before empiric antibiotics. Empiric intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam was started within the first hour given septic shock from a presumed urinary source; at 48 hours cultures grew a pan-susceptible Escherichia coli and therapy was de-escalated to intravenous ceftriaxone, with a planned 7-day total course from the day of source control and clinical response.
examination: Toxic, drowsy but rousable (GCS 13). Warm peripheries early then mottled knees. Chest clear. Abdomen soft, mild suprapubic fullness, no peritonism, no flank mass. New catheter draining turbid urine. No skin rash or eschar. No focal neurology.

labs.urinalysis: pyuria with >100 WBC/hpf, nitrite positive, bacteria +++

imaging: Bedside renal/bladder ultrasound: no hydronephrosis, no renal or perinephric collection, no obstructing stone; post-change catheter correctly sited. CT not required.
microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures and a fresh catheter-specimen urine culture (drawn after catheter replacement). At 48h: E. coli >10^5 CFU/mL in urine and E. coli in one blood-culture set; isolate pan-susceptible (susceptible to ampicillin, cephalosporins, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin; ESBL-negative). Confirms urinary source with secondary bacteraemia and permits de-escalation.
differentialDiagnoses: Complicated UTI / obstructive uropathy with urosepsis
Undifferentiated septic shock from a non-urinary source
finalDiagnosis: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CA-UTI) with secondary Gram-negative bacteraemia and septic shock
citations: IDSA Catheter-Associated UTI Diagnosis, Prevention and Treatment Guideline 2010
Surviving Sepsis Campaign Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Urinary Tract Infections and Sepsis
stewardship: Septic shock from a presumed urinary source in a patient with a chronic indwelling catheter mandates cultures then empiric broad-spectrum Gram-negative cover within the first hour (Surviving Sepsis). Piperacillin-tazobactam is a guideline-concordant empiric choice for severe CA-UTI/urosepsis, covering Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas pending susceptibilities. Source control is integral: the biofilm-laden chronic catheter must be removed or exchanged before/at antibiotic initiation. Once the pan-susceptible E. coli returned at 48h, therapy was de-escalated to ceftriaxone (narrower, once-daily, retains full activity), completing a 7-day course given prompt source control and clinical improvement. Catheter cultures should only be sent when infection is clinically suspected, and asymptomatic bacteriuria in catheterised patients must not be treated.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic aminoglycoside monotherapy given AKI unless required for resistance
Do not treat asymptomatic catheter bacteriuria
Renal dose-adjust and reassess with resolving AKI
edgeCases: If no clinical response by 48-72h or a collection is seen, image for obstruction/abscess requiring drainage
Prior ESBL/CRE colonisation or recent broad-spectrum exposure would justify empiric carbapenem instead of piperacillin-tazobactam
Persistent bacteraemia should prompt evaluation for endocarditis or an undrained focus
